### \[Create DFs, isi.mcsa columns\]

```{r create data.frames, include=FALSE}
#Combine conifer data with D1
# fd.all <- bind_rows(fd %>% select(
#   num:RH, Grass.Cure) %>%
#     mutate(Date=ymd(Date)), 
#   d1 %>% select(num:RH, Grass.Cure) %>%
#     mutate(Date=ymd(Date)))  

#assign project codes - Sharpsand
sharp <- filter(fd, str_detect(ExpProject, "Sharpsand IM")) %>% pull(num)  #original Sharpsand Immature stands only
sharp.th <- filter(fd, str_detect(ExpProject, "Sharpsand TH")) %>% pull(num)
sharp.sm <- filter(fd, str_detect(ExpProject, "Sharpsand SM")) %>% pull(num)

#get sharpsand (IM and TH) stand data
sh.fires0 <- filter(fd, num %in% c(sharp, sharp.th, sharp.sm)) %>% 
  select(fire, Date, num, ws, MC.SA, MC.SA_dens, MC.SA_season, FMC, 
         FFMC, DMC, ISI, FSG1, SFC, ROS, 
         DC, BUI, FWI, CFI1, CFI2, Site) %>%
  mutate(Exp=case_when(
           num %in% sharp ~'Imm',
           num %in% sharp.th ~'Thin',
           num %in% sharp.sm ~'Semi-M' ),
         Plot=str_extract(fire, '\\d+') %>% as.integer) #extract plot num. from string

#Recalculate mc.sa for dens=2 and dens=3 assumptions
sh.fires1 <- mutate(rowwise(sh.fires0), 
                    MC.SA2=wbmc5(ffmc=FFMC, dmc=DMC, stand=4, 
                                 density=2, season=MC.SA_season),
                    MC.SA3=ifelse(FFMC > 92.9, 
                                  wbmc5(ffmc=FFMC, dmc=DMC, stand=4, 
                                 density=2, season=MC.SA_season), 
                                 wbmc5(ffmc=FFMC, dmc=DMC, stand=4,
                                       density=3, season=MC.SA_season))) 
                #MC.SA2 assumes density of 2 for all
                #MC.SA3 assumes dens of 3 for all (except FFMC > 92.9)
                      
#Calculate isi.sa, using mcSA and wind speed:
isi.mcsa <- function(mc, ws) {
  #m = 147.2*(101-ffmc)/(59.5+ffmc)  #original mc from FFMC (mcF) formula
  f_w = exp(0.05039*ws)
  f_f = (91.9*exp(-0.1386*mc))*(1+(mc^5.31)/(4.93*10^7))
  return(0.208*f_w*f_f)
}

#main dataframe for threshold analysis - Sharpsand fires
sh.fires <- mutate(rowwise(sh.fires1), 
                isi.m=isi.mcsa(mc=MC.SA, ws=ws),  #isi.m uses actual MC.SA
                isi.m2=isi.mcsa(mc=MC.SA2, ws=ws), #alternate where all are Dens=2
                isi.m3=isi.mcsa(mc=MC.SA3, ws=ws)) %>% #alt with all Dens=3
  as.data.frame()

```

### \[VW.lf mods and lf function fc.se\]

```{r vw.lf mods, include=FALSE}
#Vw crown fire model-critical SFC
vw.sfc <- function(fmc=100, z, ros) {
  h = 460+25.9 * fmc
  I_0 = (0.01*h*z)^1.5
  #return(I_0)
  #Byram59
  sfc_0 = I_0/(300*ros)
  return(sfc_0)
  #critical sfc for crowning; needs ROS input
}

#VW model - critical surface intensity for crowning
vwi <- function(fmc=100, z) {
  h = 460+25.9 * fmc
  I_0 = (0.01*h*z)^1.5
  return(I_0)
}

#ladder fuel scaling: surface-equivalent fuel consumption (unmodified)
#changed from lf.sfc
fc.se <- function(zg, cl, fcl) {
  #zg is overstory LCBH
  #cl is ladder fuel height, or midstory fuel centroid (e.g. crown centroid of
  #an understory spruce)
  fc_se=(zg/(zg-cl))^1.5 * fcl
  return(fc_se)
}

#Isn't this wrong?? equation should be fc_se=(zg/cl)^1.5 * fcl
#No - it's correct! Since the key difference is FSG; ignition of ladder fuels
#to LCBH, not ignition of ladder fuels from ground

#save(fc.se, file='c:/Dan/_Fire_tools/rscripts/fc-se.rda')


#Assume Sharpsand FSG ~ 4.5 m
#Snag height ~ 3.2 m
#with crown ratio of 0.5, dead CBH=1.6m, centroid = 3.2-(3.2 * 0.5 * 0.5)= 
zl.test = 4.5-3.2+(3.2 * 0.5 * 0.5)  #FSG_L

```

### \[Calculate FC_L for Sharpsand plots\]

```{r get stand data calculate FC_L}
#Get original sharpsand plot data - density, snags, treatments - 18 plots, 19 fires (p11 twice)
#includes IM (ctrl), TH treatments
sh.full <- read.csv('c:/Dan/_Remote_projects/ccp_git/ccp-cfi/sharp_full.csv') %>%
  mutate(FSG=LCBH) %>%
  select(-c(X, BA, BA.d, LCBH.L)) %>%
  left_join(sh.fires %>% filter(Exp %in% c('Thin', 'Imm')), by='Plot') %>%
  select(-c(fire, Date, num, DC, FWI, CFI2, Exp)) 

#CFL values for dead ladder fuels from Stocks 1987 - IM/ctrl plots only (ones with LF)
lf.cfl <- c(0.142, 0.073, 0.313, 0.183, 0.133, 0.146, 0.131, 0.131,
              0.176, 0.182, 0.151, 0.218, 0.084) #p11 twice for 11a, 11b

#crown fuel consumption estimates by fire type
cfc.p <- c(0.39, 0.49, 0.22, 0.46)
cfc.c <- c(0.89, 1.16, 0.99, 1.27, 1.06, 1.4, 1.04, 1.03, 1.11)
cfc.s <- c(0, 0, 0.08, 0, 0)

#* 0.815# using woody consumption? use full CFL here I think; 
#ICFME surface woody consumption was 0.6 (Stocks et al 2004)
#Also recall ICFME: Stocks et al (2004): 70-86% of overstory 0-1 cm roundwood were consumed, with moisture contents from 55.5-90.4 % 
#down woody fuel moisture contents were 6.3-14.5 %

#Although P7, 18 (ctrl) and P8, 9, 16 (th) are surface fires, assume dead snags burn
dead.cfc.mean <- mean(lf.cfl)

s.ha.ctrl <- filter(sh.full, TRT=='ctrl') %>% 
  pull(s.ha.d) #stems/ha, ctrl stands
dead.cfl.snag <- mean(lf.cfl*10000/s.ha.ctrl)  #mean snag weight cfl (<1 cm) per stem, from ctrl stands; in kg/stem

lf.cflp16 <- round(6875 * dead.cfl.snag / 10000, 3)  #est. lf.cfl for p16 based on 
  #num. of snags, mean cfl (< 1 cm) per snag

sh.full$TRT[17] <- 'ctrl'  #assign partly-thinned one to ctrl grp, in line with previous Perrakis studies

lf.cfl2 <- c(0.142, 0.073, 0.313, 0.183, 0.133, 0.146, 0.131, 0.131,
              0.176, 0.182, 0.151, lf.cflp16, 0.218, 0.084) #added p16

#crown ratio equation - from Perrakis(2023) Sup analysis
sharp.cr <- function(dbh) {0.3705 + 0.009196*dbh}

#process LF in control/IM stands
sh.ctrl <- filter(sh.full, TRT=='ctrl') %>% 
  mutate(cfc.d=lf.cfl2, #dead cfc as dead cfl2
         cfc.d.stem=cfc.d * 10000/s.ha.d,   #kg/m2*10000 m2/ha/s/ha = kg/stem
         cen.l= HT.D * 0.75,  #ladder centroid of dead crown consumption; 
         #assume CR of 0.5 and full branch structure; worth testing - 
         #alternative would be HT.D *0.5 - assume CR of 1
         fc.se.ctrl=fc.se(zg=FSG, cl=cen.l, fcl=cfc.d), #calculate surface-equiv.
         #ladder fuel consumption
         fc.se.stem=fc.se.ctrl/s.ha.d,
         fc.se.ctrl2=fc.se(zg=FSG, cl=HT.D/2, fcl=cfc.d)) #alternative fc.se

#simplified df for analysis
sh.ctrl.model <-sh.ctrl %>%
  select(Plot, ISI, isi.m, FSG, SFC, cfc.d, 
         fc.se.ctrl, fc.se.ctrl2, CFI=CFI1) %>%
  mutate(sfc.final=SFC+fc.se.ctrl,
         sfc.final2=SFC+fc.se.ctrl2)

# cfc per dead stem, kg
cfc.dstem <- summarize(sh.ctrl, mean(cfc.d.stem)) %>% pull()

sh.th0 <- filter(sh.full, TRT=='th')

#Use mean values for missing data
sh.s.ha.d.th <- filter(sh.th0, !Plot %in% c(8,9)) %>%
  summarize(mean(s.ha.d)) 

#Thinned plots, mean dead stems/ha where data was missing
sh.th <- mutate(sh.th0, 
                    s.ha.d=ifelse(
                      Plot %in% c(8, 9), sh.s.ha.d.th, s.ha.d))
                        # fix s.ha.d value where no data; used to be 2600, but that was including p16


#Process LF in TH stands
sh.th <- sh.th0 %>% 
  mutate(cfc.d.stem=cfc.dstem, #use cfc per tree in ctrl plots 
         #to estimate cfc in thinned plots
         cfc.d=cfc.d.stem * s.ha.d / 10000, 
         #kg * s/ha / 10000m^2/ha to give kg/m^2
         cen.l= HT.D * 0.75,  #crown centroid calcs; assumes CR of 0.5;
         fc.se.th=fc.se(zg=FSG, cl=cen.l, fcl=cfc.d),
         fc.se.stem=fc.se.th/s.ha.d,  #surf.equivalent FC per stem
         fc.se.th2=fc.se(zg=FSG, cl=HT.D/2, fcl=cfc.d)) #alt fc.se with CR of 1

sh.th.model <- sh.th %>% select(Plot, ISI, isi.m, FSG=FSG1, SFC, fc.se.th, 
                           fc.se.th2, CFI=CFI1) %>% 
  mutate(sfc.final=SFC+fc.se.th,
         sfc.final2=SFC+fc.se.th2)


```

### \[CFI thresholds and data\]

```{r CFI Thresholds for IM TH SM plots}
#Define levels for Sharp trts:
trts <- c('Imm', 'Thin', 'Semi-M')

fires.stat <- select(sh.fires, CFI1, CFI2, FFMC, DMC, ws, SFC, 
                     MC.SA, MC.den1=MC.SA_dens, ISI, Exp, isi.m, 
                     isi.m2, isi.m3) %>%
  mutate(ExpF=factor(Exp, levels=trts)) %>%
  ungroup()
#%>%  mutate(CFI2=as.numeric(CFI2))

#CFI modelling
sh.mod <- glm(CFI1 ~ ISI + ExpF, data=fires.stat, family='binomial') #base model, ISI and treatment; both sig. at alpha=0.05

sh.mod2 <- glm(CFI1 ~ isi.m + ExpF, data=fires.stat, family='binomial') #ISI using MC.SA, density 2 for TH, 3 for others. Works! p < 0.05 for all

sh.mod2b <- glm(CFI1 ~ isi.m2 + ExpF, data=fires.stat, family='binomial') 
#isi.m2 has MC.SA_dens=2 for all

sh.mod3 <- glm(CFI1 ~ isi.m3 + ExpF, data=fires.stat, family='binomial')
#dens3 for all except FFMC > 92.9

#Used sh.mod (ISI) for log. regression graph
#Use both for threshold values

#graph with jittered scatter plot
#Isi.seq <- seq(4, 20, by=0.1)

#which model to use? sh.mod with ISI or sh.mod2 with mc.sa or other
use.mod <- sh.mod
use.mod2 <- sh.mod2b
use.mod3 <- sh.mod3

#generate fake data for log. regression graphs
fdata.IM <- data.frame(fISI=seq(3, 20, by=0.1), fExp='Imm') %>%
  mutate(CFI=predict.glm(use.mod, 
                         newdata=list(ISI=fISI, ExpF=fExp), 
                         type='response'))
                         #newdata=list(isi.m=fISI, ExpF=fExp), 
                         #type='response'))
                         
fdata.SM <- data.frame(fISI=seq(3, 20, by=0.1), fExp='Semi-M') %>%
  mutate(CFI=predict.glm(use.mod, 
                         newdata=list(ISI=fISI, ExpF=fExp), 
                         type='response'))
                         #newdata=list(isi.m=fISI, ExpF=fExp), 
                         #type='response'))

fdata.TH <- data.frame(fISI=seq(3, 20, by=0.1), fExp='Thin') %>%
  mutate(CFI=predict.glm(use.mod, 
                         newdata=list(ISI=fISI, ExpF=fExp), 
                         type='response'))
                         #newdata=list(isi.m=fISI, ExpF=fExp), 
                         #ype='response'))

mod.co<-use.mod$coefficients
mod2.co<-use.mod2$coefficients

#solve for p=0.5 in logistical function; 
#p=exp(b0+b1*ISI+b2*ExpSemi-M+b3*ExpThin)
#so 0.5=1/(1+exp(b0+b1*ISI+b2*ExpSemi-M+b3*ExpThin)
#2=1+exp(b0...)
#1=exp()
#0=b0+b1*ISI+b2*ExpSemi-M+b3*ExpThin
#ISI=(b0+b2*ExpSemi-M+b3*ExpThin)/b1

#for isi.m
#0=b0+b1*isi.m+b2*ExpThin+b3*ExpSemi-M+c
```

### \[CFI graph\]

```{r Log-CFI graph, define functions}
#get cf thresholds (p=0.5); see prev. code chunk for derivation
#With ISI model:
isi.thresh.im <-  
  -(mod.co[[1]])/mod.co[[2]]  #
  
isi.thresh.semiM <- 
  -(mod.co[[1]] + mod.co[[4]])/mod.co[[2]]

isi.thresh.th <- 
  -(mod.co[[1]] + mod.co[[3]])/mod.co[[2]]

#with isi.m model:
isim.thresh.im <-  
  -(mod2.co[[1]])/mod2.co[[2]]  #
  
isim.thresh.semiM <- 
  -(mod2.co[[1]] + mod2.co[[4]])/mod2.co[[2]]

isim.thresh.th <- 
  -(mod2.co[[1]] + mod2.co[[3]])/mod2.co[[2]]

  
#thresholds with ISI (sh.mod):
#imm: 6.61
#th: 10.31
#semi-M: 8.62

#thresholds with ISI.mcsa (sh.mod2):
#imm: 4.70
#th: 9.19
#semi-M: 8.95

#'working mean':
#'imm': 5.7
#'th': 9.8

#set colours properly
col.levels <- c('Imm'='purple3',
                'Semi-M'='orange',
                'Thin'='turquoise2')

#Main ISI-CFI graph with jittered data, for 3 treatments 
sh.isi.log <- 
  ggplot(fires.stat, aes(y=CFI1, x=isi.m))+
  #scale_shape_manual(values=c(23, 22, 21)) +   #pick nice shapes 
  theme_classic() +
  scale_shape_manual(values=c(21, 23)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(fill=Exp, colour=Exp, shape=CFI2), 
              size=2.5, width=0, height = 0.02, alpha=0.4) +  
  geom_line(data=fdata.IM, aes(x=fISI, y=CFI, colour='Imm')) +
  geom_line(data=fdata.SM, aes(x=fISI, y=CFI, colour='Semi-M')) +
  geom_line(data=fdata.TH, aes(x=fISI, y=CFI, colour='Thin')) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=col.levels, aesthetics=c('colour', 'fill')) +
  labs(x='ISI', y='p(CFO)', colour='Exp', fill='Exp') +
  annotate('segment', x=isi.thresh.im, xend=isi.thresh.im, #little vert line, im
           y=0.4, yend=0.6, alpha=0.4, colour='purple3') +
  annotate('segment', x=isi.thresh.th, xend=isi.thresh.th, #vert line, th 
           y=0.4, yend=0.6, alpha=0.6, colour='turquoise2')+
  annotate('segment', x=isi.thresh.im-0.75, xend=isi.thresh.im+0.75,

  annotate('segment', x=isi.thresh.th-0.75, xend=isi.thresh.th+0.75,
```

### \[M calculations\]

```{r m.calculations, include=FALSE}

#t-test to compare SFC between treatments
#t.test(sh.ctrl$SFC, sh.th$SFC)
#p=0.1409

#t-test to compare DMC between treatments
#t.test(sh.ctrl$DMC, sh.th$DMC)
#p=0.3515

#m formula
#M=SFCx(ROS_th - ROS_im)/(ROS_im x FC_se_im)

#FC_se_im; -7 is to avoid duplicating p11- ok, not needed
fc.se.im.mean <- mean(sh.ctrl$fc.se.ctrl)

#solve for M function
m.function <- function(sfc, ros.th, ros.im, fc.se.im) { 
  m=sfc*(ros.th-ros.im)/(ros.im*fc.se.im)
  return(m)
  #solve for m with IM and TH threshold values
}

#model list - ISI, updated since Surf Fire paper
#List to use, ISI: m12, m16, m20
#to use, ISI.sa: m11c, m13, m17

#Prepare vectors for modelling
isi.vals <- c(isi.thresh.im, isi.thresh.th)
isim.vals <-c(isim.thresh.im, isim.thresh.th)
ffmc.val <- mean(sh.full$FFMC)  #90.89
dmc.val <- mean(sh.full$DMC)   #42
ws.vals <- c(6.055, 14.881)  #ws vals at FFMC 90.89 to get thresh ISI
sfc.mean <- mean(sh.full$SFC)  #1.3374
mcsa.val <- mean(sh.full$MC.SA2) #10.329 , using Density=2 for all
ws.vals.sa <- c(5.493, 13.883)  #ws vals at mc.sa 10.329 to get thresh isim

#Model predictions at crown fire thresholds: ISI models
#
Mm20 <- m20(ws.vals) #ok with FFMC 90.89
Mm12 <- fun.m12(isi.vals) #ok ISI
Mm16 <- fun.m16(ws=ws.vals, mc=mcF(ffmc.val)) #maybe

#Variable types
vars <- c('ROS: WS', 'ROS: ISI', 'ROS: WS, FFMC')

#nice simple table of ROS, ISI models
modelMms <- rbind(Mm20, Mm12, Mm16) %>% #no m18
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(Variable=vars)

colnames(modelMms) <- c('ROS.im', 'ROS.th', 'Method')

#Model predictions at CF thresholds: ISI.sa models
#
Mm11c <- fun.m11c(isi.m=isim.vals)
Mm13 <- fun.m13(isi.m=isim.vals)
Mm17 <- fun.m17(ws=ws.vals.sa, mcsa=mcsa.val)

#Var types
vars2 <- c('ROS: ISI_sa1', 'ROS: ISI_sa2', 'ROS: WS, mc_sa')

modelMmsa <- rbind(Mm11c, Mm13, Mm17) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(Var=vars2)

colnames(modelMmsa) <- c('ROS.im', 'ROS.th', 'Method')

solve.for.m1 <- mutate(modelMms, 
                        M=m.function(sfc=sfc.mean, ros.th=ROS.th,
                              ros.im=ROS.im, fc.se.im=fc.se.im.mean))
#works!
#Mean of 5.23

solve.for.m2 <- mutate(modelMmsa, 
                        M=m.function(sfc=sfc.mean, ros.th=ROS.th,
                              ros.im=ROS.im, fc.se.im=fc.se.im.mean))

m.table0 <- full_join(solve.for.m1, solve.for.m2) %>%
  select(Method, everything()) %>%
  tibble()

#Another way is with M7, M9, using SFC (M7: ISI; M9: ISI.sa)
#Updated Aug 5
#TH threshold ROS with ISI
#TH threshold ROS is reached (m7) using IM ISI with SFC of 5.1796
#this is mean SFC + FC.se*M
#M=(5.1796-1.337)/FC.se
#TH threshold ROS is reached using IM isim with SFC of 5.604 (not updated for m9c)
#this is mean SFC + FC.se*M
#M=(5.604-1.337)/FC.se
#M=6.64 #old value
#
m7beta1 <- summary(m7.sros.ISI2SFC.mod)$coefficients[1]
m7beta2 <- summary(m7.sros.ISI2SFC.mod)$coefficients[2]
Mm7 <- (((m7beta1 * isi.thresh.th^2+m7beta2*sqrt(sfc.mean)-m7beta1*isi.thresh.im^2)/m7beta2)^2-sfc.mean)/fc.se.im.mean
#5.9817

beta1 <- summary(m9c)$coefficients[1]
beta2 <- summary(m9c)$coefficients[2]
Mm9 <- (((beta1*isim.thresh.th^2+beta2*sqrt(sfc.mean)-beta1*isim.thresh.im^2)/beta2)^2-sfc.mean)/fc.se.im.mean
#6.611

#

#Updated? Don't recall where this comes from
expert1 <- 8.62818
expert2 <- 6.73126

solve.expert <- data.frame(Method=c('Expert 1', 'Expert 2'), 
                           ROS.im=NA, ROS.th=NA, M=c(expert1, expert2))

solve.m7 <- data.frame(Method='ROS & SFC 1', ROS.im=NA, ROS.th=NA, M=Mm7)
solve.m9 <- data.frame(Method='ROS & SFC 2', ROS.im=NA, ROS.th=NA, M=Mm9)

#Table with all M estimates
m.table <- bind_rows(solve.expert, solve.m7, solve.m9, m.table0) %>%
  as_tibble()

grand.mean.M <- m.table %>% summarize(mean(M))
#6.12
#
#Should also make same calcs for CR=1
#Also, correct IM FC.se by subtracting mean FC_L in TH stands

m.table
```

### \[Empirical crown fire reanalysis\]

## Abstract

Predicting the onset of conifer crown fires is uncertain, though canopy
fuel structure has been shown to influence the crowning process. Ladder
fuels (LF) are flammable biomass elements that act as a bridge between
surface and canopy layers. While LF elements are suspected of being
disproportionately important in crown fire initiation, they are
difficult to quantify and incorporate into prediction systems. A
somewhat similar problem occurs with multi-story canopy fuels, whereby
ignition of subcanopy layers is first required in order for overstory
elements to become involved. By rearranging the terms of a well-known
model, crown fire initiation is reframed as a critical fuel consumption
(FC)-driven process. A new equation evaluates FC at varying heights
above ground, allowing for LF analysis using the surface-equivalent fuel
consumption, *FC~SE~*. Since surface fuels and LF greatly differ in
structure, we also tested a calibration multiplier, *M*, using field
data from Canadian experimental fires. Estimated values of *M* were
derived using three methods, with an overall mean of approximately *M*=
`r round(grand.mean.M, 1)` indicating six-fold influence of LF
consumption compared to surface FC. These findings and equations will
allow for important improvements to crown fire prediction and will
greatly increase the effectiveness of hazard reduction treatments.

## 1. Introduction

Conifer forests cover most of the circumboreal region of the world and
crown fires represent a significant fire-related hazard in these stands
[@kneeshaw2011; @stocks1991]. Surface fires rarely spread \> 6 m/min
under closed conifer canopies [@kiil1976; @perrakis2026], as higher
spread rates are usually associated with canopy fire involvement in the
form of torching or crowning behaviour. Once flames reach the upper
reaches of the canopy, they are much more subject to influence by free
air in the lower atmosphere. The fully developed crowning process has
long been known to be associated with a dramatic increase in fire spread
rate, due to several processes including flame tilt, increased lee-side
wind exposure and vigorous short-range ember spotting [@taylor2004;
@alexander2016]. Predicting the initiation of crown fires is therefore
critical to accurate fire behaviour forecasting in conifer forests.

Stand structure is well-known to influence crown fire tendency. Models
of crown fire initiation (CFI) or occurrence identify the height to the
crown base as a critical structure variable; stands with a lower crown
base, including species such as spruce (*Picea* sp.) or true fir
(*Abies* sp.), are more easily ignited by an equivalent surface fire
than higher-crown stands [@vanwagner1977a; @cruz2006; @perrakis2023b].
While higher crown base stands, such as those of pine (*Pinus* sp.) or
coastal Douglas-fir (*Pseudotsuga* *menziesii*) often require more
extreme weather conditions and higher surface fire intensity for canopy
ignition, this can be facilitated by so-called ladder fuels (LF). This
term refers to any easily-ignited fuels in the mid-canopy space, meaning
fine-textured and flammable dead and live biomass above the surface fuel
complex but below the live canopy base. In Canada, early wildfire
researcher J.G. Wright first noted nearly a century ago that 'crown
fires are not likely to occur unless there is a large volume of fuel
under the trees' [@wright1932]. Decades later, Van Wagner
[@vanwagner1977a] described his classic crown fire initiation (CFI)
model based on empirical data and physical convection theory, noting
that such 'bridge fuels' consisted of 'combustible matter such as loose
bark, dead lower branches, lichen, small conifers, etc.' located above
the surface fuel complex; such fuels needed to be 'present in sufficient
quantity to intensify the surface fire appreciably as well as to extend
the flame height'. While Van Wagner's model has been widely cited,
adapted, and incorporated into operational fire prediction systems,
practical methods for quantifying the LF influence are still lacking
nearly a half–century later.

We presently begin our analysis with the simple and well-known
formulation of Van Wagner's model, originally developed to identify the
critical surface fire intensity ($I_0$) to enable CFI:

$$
I_0=(chz)^{1.5}
$$

\[eq. 1\], where $h$ is heat of ignition, $z$ is live crown base height
(LCBH), and $c$ is a dimensional constant, derived empirically.
Alexander and Cruz [@alexander2016] have noted that the $c$ value is
somewhat questionable and may be stand-dependent. Most modelling systems
have combined $I_0$ with Byram's [-@byram1959] fireline intensity
equation in order to solve for critical rate of spread. This combination
has allowed for linkages with Rothermel's [-@rothermel1972]
semi-physical surface rate of spread model [e.g. @scott2001;
@andrews2014], or with empirical rate of spread (ROS) functions, such as
in the FBP System [@forestrycanadafiredangergroup1992]. Surprisingly, a
simple algebraic rearranging of the terms of Van Wagner's model allows
for a useful and powerful estimator applicable to LF elements at varying
heights above ground. Empirical data presently allows for calibration of
the theoretical and conceptual linkages between surface and crown fire
processes.

### 1.1 Objective

The objectives of this study were to 1) present a theoretical framework
for analyzing LF influence in crown fire initiation, as previously
described in draft form [@perrakis2025b]; and 2) calibrate and evaluate
the theoretical equation with field data. These goals will allow for
much greater flexibility for adapting real world stand structure into
crown fire models and systems.

### 1.2 Theoretical model: vertical scaling of ladder fuel consumption

Ladder fuels are defined by their fine texture and intermediate vertical
position [@vanwagner1977a; @kilgore1975]. If *z* represents vertical
position above the forest floor in a conifer stand, LF exist between the
surface fuels, at $z=0$, and canopy fuels, which for our purposes begin
at the live canopy base height (LCBH), typically measured or estimated
at heights of \~1–12 m or so in boreal or hemi-boreal forests. When
continuous with the surface fuelbed and ignited by a proximate source
(i.e. an advancing fireline), the heat flux contribution of LF fuels
[@melnik2022] is often much closer to the canopy base, and therefore
much more likely to contribute to canopy ignition compared to similar
fuel quantities at the surface.

It was previously shown [@perrakis2025b] that the formulation of the Van
Wagner [-@vanwagner1977a] crown initiation model enables an algebraic
equivalency between fuel consumption and the inverse of *z* (LCBH). The
equations will be presently reviewed for clarity. Replacing $I_0$
(eq. 1) with Byram's [-@byram1959] fireline intensity formula produces
the following popular transformation [e.g.,
@forestrycanadafiredangergroup1992; @scott2001]:

$$
H \cdot SFC \cdot ROS=(c \cdot h)^{1.5} z^{1.5}  
$$

\[eq. 2\], where $H$ is the heat of combustion, $SFC$ is surface fuel
consumption, and $ROS$ is rate of forward spread. In addition to solving
for critical ROS for crown fire initiation [@vanwagner1977a;
@alexander1988a], this can also be solved for critical SFC:

$$
SFC_0=\frac {(ch)^{1.5} z^{1.5}} {H \cdot ROS} 
$$

\[eq. 3\]. Since we are interested in varying the vertical position of
fuel elements, we can compare different LCBH levels, $z_1$ and $z_2$,
holding all other variables equal:

$$
\frac {SFC_2}{SFC_1}=
\frac {  \left[  \frac {(ch)^{1.5} z_2^{1.5}} {H \cdot ROS} \right] } 
{  \left[  \frac {(ch)^{1.5} z_1^{1.5}} {H \cdot ROS} \right] }
$$

\[eq. 4\], assuming no change in ROS with varying LCBH. This simplifies
to a more basic relationship between fuel consumption at different
heights beneath a flammable canopy:

$$
SFC_2=(\frac {z_2} {z_1})^{1.5} \cdot SFC_1
$$

\[eq. 5\]. In the case of the consumption of an elevated LF quantity
$FC_L$, positioned at a certain height above ground $C_L$ (ladder fuel
centroid), the surface-equivalent $FC$ value ($FC_{SE}$) is defined
using a modification of eq. 5, where the influence of $FC_L$ represents
an inflated consumption quantity due to its elevated position and
therefore disproportional influence on crown fire. In this case, $z$
remains the normal LCBH for the live canopy and $z-C_L$ represents the
fuel strata gap between LF elements and the LCBH, the key vertical gap
in this situation for representing the LF influence:

$$
FC_{SE}=(\frac {z} {z-C_L})^{1.5} \cdot FC_L ~~, ~~~~~~ z > C_L
$$

\[eq. 6\]. Using Equation 6, it becomes possible to estimate the
contribution of canopy fuel elements and compare them with the surface
fuel complex in an additive manner.

There are several concerns with this relationship that must be addressed
before it can be inserted into a crown fire initiation or occurrence
model: 1) an adequate estimate of $FC_L$ must be available, likely from
a previous study or model, and obtaining this information is clearly
non-trivial. 2) Eq. 6 treats LF and surface fuel structure and
combustion properties identically, despite obvious structure
differences; surface fuels in forested systems tend to have much greater
bulk density and therefore lower pososity and airflow compared with
canopy fuels [@rothermel1972; @schwilk2015; @keane2015]. This concern is
also related to the available data on SFC and head fire intensity, such
as from systems and datasets which assume that all consumed surface and
ground fuels contribute to surface fire intensity [@vanwagner1977a;
@forestrycanadafiredangergroup1992]; this notion likely overemphasizes
dense duff fuels that burn in post-frontal combustion, as the notion of
flame residence time [@cheney1990] is ignored. In contrast, fine canopy
and ladder fuel strata are much more aerated and discontinuous. This
difference between surface and LF structure will presently be addressed
via empirical calibration. A final concern is 3) ladder fuel height
cannot exceed the LCBH (Eq. 6), and when the vertical difference
diminishes, $FC_{SE}$ can reach extreme values. Either calibration or
some estimated working limits may also be needed to account for this
constraint.

### 1.3 Ladder fuel multiplier

A simple approach to the challenge of contrasting aerated ladder fuel
complexes with dense surface fuel beds is to use a multiplier. This
quantity would be used on $FC_{SE}$ in order to bring it in line with
SFC values. We will presently evaluate this approach, with the relevant
equation $SFC=FC_{SE} \cdot M$ \[eq. 7\], with $M$ being the LF
multiplier, derived using primarily empirical means.

Measured and estimated SFC values in Canadian experimental conifer fires
ranged from 0.2 to 3.8 kg m^-2^ [@perrakis2023b]. Ladder fuel
consumption (*FC~L~*) data is much rarer and will often require some
assumptions or models to estimate. The value of the multiplier, $M$,
clearly depends on the nature of the SFC and *FC~L~* being used, but
could range from 1 (no effect) to 10 or more for order of magnitude
differences in structure influence.

The remainder of the study tests and discusses the estimate of *M*,
followed by a further testing phase by modifying a crown fire model.

## 2. Methods

Three separate validation methods were used to evaluate the theoretical
ladder fuel scaling relationship (Eq. 6) and calibrate the multiplier
*M*. All three methods rely on the valuable experiments and ensuing data
collected conducted at Sharpsand Creek, Ontario, in the 1970s –1990s,
discussed below (Sec. 2.1). First, a crown fire threshold was identified
between three treatment types. The threshold was then used to for
calibration, using 2) an SFC-based ROS model as well as 3) additional
models calibrated using Byram's intensity equation. The inclusion of
ladder fuels as well as the estimated *M* value were further evaluated
using a sensitivity analysis of a refitted crown fire occurrence model.
The final step leads to a new concept of crown fire, where flaming
transitions between canopy fuel strata can be tested and defined
individually. All of these relate to stand level estimates of fuel
structure using mean measured values. These techniques are relatively
simple and operationally practical, but may mask significant impacts of
within-stand heterogeneity and spatial pattern of fuel arrangement (e.g.
clumping, proximity to overstory trees, etc.).

### 2.1 Study area: Sharpsand Creek, Ontario

The validation made use of data from the fire experiments at Sharpsand
Creek, Ontario. This site and its observations have been analyzed in
several studies but remain useful for the present purposes. As
previously described, 27 plots in three separate treatment types were
burned between 1974 and 1991 at this site north of Thessalon, Ontario.
The original unaltered stand (immature: IM) consisted of naturally
regenerated jack pine following a 1948 wildfire, with dense stocking of
a single live cohort along with abundant standing dead stems forming
volatile ladder fuels [@walker1975; @stocks1973]. Results from the
initial experimental fires (1975-1981) were published by Stocks
[-@stocks1987] and formed the empirical basis for much of the FBP System
C-4 fuel type [@forestrycanadafiredangergroup1992]. These observations
were also analyzed separately by Van Wagner [@vanwagner1993] and used in
additional fire behaviour studies [@call1997; @albini1986; @cruz1999;
@cruz2003b].

During the course of the early experiments, it was discovered that 5 or
6 of the plots had been hand-thinned (TH) in 1960, removing most of the
dead stems and resulting in much less dense stands compared with the
'control' IM plots [@stocks1987; B. J. Stocks, personal communication,
Jan. 2020]. Thinned stands were measured to have higher DBH than
controls [@degroot2022]. It is unclear whether thinning resulted in
increased height or altered LCBH compared with than controls. Any
treatment differences in LCBH would be small, as experimental leaders
did not observe it and originally assigned the approximate LCBH value of
4 m to all experimental plots, including controls and thinned plots
(B.J. Stocks, personal communication 2020).

In the later fires (1988-1991), stand characteristics and fuel structure
had already changed from the earlier experiments, reflecting natural
post-fire succession [@brown2026]. The dense IM plots were initially
surveyed at \>9000 live stems ha^-1^ and \> 10,000 dead stems ha^-1^
[measured in 1973; @stocks1987]; when re-surveyed in 1984, self-thinning
in so-called semi-mature (SM) stands [@mcrae2017] had reduced live and
dead stem density by 53 % and 63 %, respectively, while total basal area
increased by 37 %; mean estimated LCBH had also increased to 5.3 m,
about 1 m higher than IM stands [@mcrae2017].

Previous studies handled these three stand types in various ways
[@perrakis2023b]. While the IM stands were included in the C-4 fuel
type, the TH plots had been deemed more representative of mature pine
stand structure and included in the FBP System C-3 fuel type; this
despite similar age, LCBH and site characteristics as the IM stands
[@degroot2022]. In later studies, the ladder fuel influence in IM stands
was estimated by some authors to act similarly to a reduction of the
LCBH; this was based on the logic of reduced distance between surface
fuel and continuous canopy fuel caused by the standing dead ladder
fuels. This modified LCBH measure was termed the Fuel Strata Gap, equal
to 2 m [@cruz2004a; @cruz2006; @perrakis2023b]. The raw Sharpsand Creek
fire data along with descriptions of fire type label classes and
interpretations can be found in supplemental material.

### 2.2 Crowning behaviour and ladder fuel consumption

The most challenging value for the analysis is the fuel consumption of
ladder fuels, as this is seldom measured (though sometimes estimated
indirectly) in experimental studies. Stocks [-@stocks1987] presented
estimated dead roundwood fuel consumption for the original Sharpsand
Creek experimental fires, and these values are used presently.

For this analysis, ladder fuel influence was quantified using equation 6
to scale the estimated ladder fuel consumption (dead canopy fuel \< 1
cm; Stocks 1987) into an equivalent SFC contribution value, $SFC_L$. The
vertical position of fine standing ladder fuels was assumed to be the
crown centroid of the mean dead snag canopy layer at the stand level:

$$C_L=CBH_{sap}+\frac {height_{sap}-CBH_{sap}}{2}$$\[eq. 8\]
[@perrakis2023b]; $CBH_{sap}$ and $height_{sap}$ are the mean crown base
height and mean height of the dead saplings, respectively. However,
since $CBH_{sap}$ was unknown in our Sharpsand calibration dataset, we
first assumed a crown ratio [CR; @holdaway1986] of 0.5; to test the
sensitivity of this assumption, we did a second analysis with a CR of 1.

#### 2.2.1 Estimation 1 - Expert opinion, Sharpsand Creek (ON)

The first calibration method involved expert opinion from previous
studies. As noted above, Cruz et al. [-@cruz2004a] estimated that the
abundant ladder fuels characterizing the Sharpsand Creek stands, in the
form of standing dead trees (including dead branches, bark flakes, and
fine stemwood) amounted to a 'fuel strata gap' of 2 m, compared to
approximately 4 m for the actual LCBH (*z*). We used those values as a
first estimate along with equation 5 to investigate a potential value
for multiplier M.

#### 2.2.2 Estimations 2 and 3 - Analyis of crowning thresholds, Sharpsand Creek (ON)

For the second and third estimation methods, we used the Sharpsand
Creek, Ontario experiments once again, including the full complement of
immature (IM), thinned (TH), and semi-mature (SM) treatments in our
analysis [@stocks1987; @mcrae2017; @perrakis2023b]. This site, with many
fires in stands that differed primarily by age (time since wildfire) and
treatment, provided the ideal test case for assessing threshold crown
fire conditions and ladder fuel effects. We used logistic regression to
identify the crown fire thresholds between weather indices and
treatments. This was initially done using the initial spread index
(*ISI*) from the FWI System [@vanwagner1987]; we also tested for
thresholds using a stand-adjusted version of the ISI ($ISI_{sa}$), which
was simply the ISI equation's f(F) function fitted to Wotton and
Beverly's [@wotton2007] stand-adjusted moisture content ($mc_{sa}$)
[@perrakis2026].

We then evaluated the crowning thresholds in terms of critical FC to
solve for the multiplier effect (*M*) using two different approaches.
Method 2 involved using an SFC-based ROS model and the different SFC
values required under identical fire weather conditions (*ISI~sa~*) to
equalize ROS, based on eq. 7. Method 3 involved the additional step of
using Byram's [-@byram1959] fireline intensity along with predicted ROS
using fitted surface ROS models, and solving for *M* using the threshold
values.

#### 2.2.3 Evaluation using a crown fire model \[incomplete\]

For the final method of examining the theoretical relationships, we
returned to a recent crown fire analysis and attemped to refit the
relationship between fire environment variables and crown fire
occurrence. As in Perrakis et al. [-@perrakis2023b], we used 10 m open
wind speed, estimated litter and fine dead surface fuel moisture (as
represented by either the FFMC or the stand-adjusted moisture content,
$mc_{sa}$). This time, rather than subjectively estimating the FSG
adjustments to LCBH in certain stands, we used eq. 7 to estimate the
ladder fuel contributions of standing dead fuels, based on the measured
or estimated \< 1 cm elevated roundwood (dead) consumption values. We
tested only the best-performing model forms for this purpose, which had
log-transformed SFC values and a 3/2 exponent for the LCBH term. The
multiplier *M* in this case was held inside the log-transformed SFC
term; thus, the respective coefficient was fitted to
$log(SFC+FC_{SE} \cdot M)$. The initial value of M in this fitted model
was taken from the previous estimates, but a sensitivity analysis step
also tested several other values of M in addition to the mean calibrated
value.

## 3. Results

#### 3.1 Estimating *M* multiplier - Method 1, Expert opinion

The first estimation method for the multiplier M was based on solving
eq. 5 using the expert opinion values given in Cruz et al. [@cruz2004a;
@cruz2005] to account for ladder fuels.

From eq. 5, we can easily rearrange as follows, assuming $SFC_1=SFC_2$:

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac {SFC_2} {SFC_1+FC_L \cdot M} &= (\frac {z_2} {z_1})^{1.5} \\
M&= \frac {SFC \cdot (z_1-z_2)^{1.5}} {FC_L \cdot z_2^{1.5}} \\
\end{aligned}$$

\[eq. 9\]. Starting with the approximate LCBH values originally reported
for the Sharpsand IM stands (*z~1~*= 4 m), this value was reduced by 2 m
to produce the FSG estimate (*z~2~*=2 m). The mean estimated *FC~L~* of
the IM plots was 0.155 kg m^-2^, and mean *SFC* was 1.337. Therefore, we
solve eq. 9 for our first *M* estimate:

$$\begin{aligned}
M
&=\frac {1.337 \cdot (4-2)^{1.5}} {0.155 \cdot 2^{1.5}} \\
M&=8.63 \end{aligned}$$. The same calculation was also completed with
more precise values derived from original stand data [@walker1975].
Detailed plot-level analyses [@perrakis2023b] produced mean
treatment-level LCBH values of 4.36 m in the IM plots. Solving eq. 8
with $z_1=4.36$ and $z_2=2.36$ (following the assumption of
$FSG=z_2=z_1-2$) produces a slightly lower estimate of $M=6.731$.

#### 3.2 Crowning thresholds and critical ROS, Sharpsand Creek

The second multiplier estimation method involved the logistic regression
between treatments. The full dataset consisted of 27 experimental fires:
14 IM, 5 TH, and 8 SM treatments. These tests revealed ISI treatment as
significant predictors (⍺=0.05), and ISIsa and treatment as possibly
significant predictors (⍺=0.1) of crown fire occurrence.

##### 3.2.1 Critical ROS for crowning

Crowning thresholds were `r round(isi.thresh.im, 2)` and
`r round(isi.thresh.th, 2)` ISI for IM (control) and TH (thinned)
stands, respectively. In terms of *ISI~SA~*, the respective thresholds
were `r round(isim.thresh.im, 2)` and `r round(isim.thresh.th, 2)` for
IM and TH stands.

```{r}
sh.isi.log
```

Approaches for solving for M also involved several ROS models, as
previously noted, and a range of algebraic solutions.

##### 3.2.2 *M* Method 2 - SFC-based sROS model

The second method used to estimate *M* involved using Perrakis et al.'s
[-@perrakis2026] ROS Model 9, which uses the *ISI~sa~* and *SFC* as
inputs. The reasoning is that the difference between the *ISI~sa~* ROS
thresholds for IM and TH stands could be explained by the transformed
SFC term representing *FC~L~*, the ladder fuel consumption. This method
does not require a transformation to Byram's intensity, as the ROS model
itself is partly based on SFC.

Mean $SFC_{Im}$ was 1.414 kg m^-2^, while mean $SFC_{Th}$ was 1.124 kg
m^-2^, with the difference being non-significant (t-test: *P*=0.141).
Starting with the IM value threshold *ISI~sa~* (6.053) and the mean SFC
(1.337), the estimated ROS ($\hat{ROS_{IM}}$) using Model 9 is 1.226 m
min^-1^. This can be calculated using the M9 ROS model parameters
[@perrakis2026]:

$$ \hat{ROS_{IM}}=\beta_1 ISI_{sa,0}^{~~~2} + \beta_2 SFC^{0.5} $$

\[eq. 11\], where \\beta1 and \\beta2 are the fitted M9 model estimates,
0.01474 and 0.5929, respectively. A similar equation can be written to
express the estimated threshold ROS in the TH stands: $\hat{ROS_{TH}}=$
1.944 m min^-1^. Rather than varying ISIsa, we can also increase the M9
ROS estimate with higher SFC. Thus, at some higher SFC value, SFC',
$\hat{ROS_{TH}}$ is predicted even with the lower ISIsa value, ISIsa.0,
IM: $\hat{ROS_{0 \cdot TH}}=f(ISI_{sa \cdot0, IM}, SFC')$ \[eq. 12\].

By replacing SFC' in eq. 12 with eq. 7, we can solve for M in this
manner (this can also be estimated iteratively using a programmed ROS
function for M9):

$$ \begin{aligned}
\beta_1 ISI_{sa \cdot 0, IM}^{~~~2}+\beta_2(SFC+FC_{SE} \cdot M)^{0.5} 
&= 
\beta_1ISI_{sa \cdot 0, TH}^{~~~2}+\beta_2(SFC)^{0.5}\\
M&=\frac {\frac {(\beta_1ISI_{sa \cdot 0, TH}^{~~~2} + \beta_2(SFC)^{0.5}-
\beta_1ISI_{sa \cdot 0, IM}^{~~~2})^2}{\beta_2} -SFC} {FC_{SE}} \\
\end{aligned}
 $$

In this case, we calculate ladder fuel height ($C_L$) using an estimated
crown ratio of 0.5 and cohort heights from Walker and Stocks'
[-@walker1975] original stand data. Mean dead sapling height and \< 1 cm
dead consumption (*FC~L~*) in control stands were 3.49 m and 0.159 kg
m^-2^, resulting in mean *C~L~*=2.62 m. *FC~SE~* (eq. 6) ranged from
0.291 to 1.227 kg m^-2^, with a mean of `r fc.se.im.mean` kg m^-2^ .
Using the fitted M9 coefficients, mean SFC, and mean *FC~SE~* for IM
stands as the \< 1 cm dead roundwood (eq. 6), this second method
estimates *M* = 6.64.

##### 3.2.3 *M* Method 3 - sROS models and Byram's intensity

The third method relies on estimated threshold surface ROS values and
several ROS models based on weather alone, together with Byram's fire
intensity equation [@byram1959]. These calculations assume that
equivalent critical surface intensity values ($I_0$) are required for
crowning in the control and thinned stands, both with dense canopies and
LCBH of about 4.4 m.

The equivalency between the critical surface intensity and critical ROS
($ROS_0$) in the IM and TH stands is expressed as follows:

$$\begin{align*}
I_{0 \cdot Im} &= I_{0 \cdot Th} \\
h \cdot SFC_{Im} \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Im} &= h \cdot SFC_{Th} \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Th} \\
(SFC+FC_{SE \cdot Im} \cdot M) \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Im} &= SFC_{Th} \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Th} \\
\end{align*}
$$

Using the SFC and FC~SE~ values described above, with ROS estimated from
the IM and TH crown fire thresholds, M can be estimated as follows:

$$\begin{align*}
(SFC_{Im}+FC_{SE \cdot Im} \cdot M) \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Im} &= SFC_{Th} \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Th} \\
M &= \frac {SFC_{Th} \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Th} - {SFC_{Im} \cdot ROS_{0 \cdot Im}}} {ROS_{Im} \cdot FC_{SE \cdot Im}} \\
\end{align*}
$$ \[eq. 9\], or, if we assume that $SFC_{Th}=SFC_{Im}$,
$$ M=\frac {SFC(ROS_{Th}-ROS_{Im})} {ROS_{Im} \cdot FC_{SE \cdot Im}}$$
\[eq. 10\]. Using the overall mean SFC of 1.337 kg m^-2^, two ROS models
produced $$\begin{align*} 
M_{ISI} &= \frac {1.337 (2.862-0.746)} {0.746 \cdot 0.642}  \\
&= 5.910 \\
\end{align*}
$$

using the ISI-based sROS model M12 and crowning thresholds, and
$$\begin{align*}
M_{ISI_{sa}} &= \frac {1.337(1.901-0.6097)} {0.6097 \cdot 0.642}\\
&= 4.409\\
\end{align*}
$$

using the ISI~SA~-based sROS model M13 and the two threshold ISI~SA~
values. Additional ROS models were also tested, producing some variation
in M values (Table x). The overall mean M value was
`r grand.mean.M %>% round(2)` .

In addition varying sROS models, the sensitivity analysis also tested
crown ratio (CR) by using the the dead ladder fuel midpoint (cohort
height/2), the equivalent of a crown ratio of 1. This results in
significantly lower FC~SE~ values, due to the greater z~L~ values. The
varied sROS and CR models resulted in the matrix of M estimates shown in
Table X. \[to complete\]

#### Empirical crown fire analysis \[not sure if we include\]

\[Not yet updated\] Finally, we reanalyzed the experimental crown fire
dataset using Monte Carlo cross-validation, comparing models with
$log(SFC)$, $log(SFC + FC_{SE})$, and $log(SFC + FC_{SE} \cdot M)$. The
starting value for M was 4 \[to update and redo\], a rough mean of the
previous estimates.

As show in the table, the cross-validation evidence supports the
existence of M \> 1. Both the FFMC- and MC~SA~-based models (7, 8) using
M had higher mean accuracy and lower AIC than comparable models
incorporating ladder fuels without a multiplier effect (5, 6). The best
models were superior than either the base (LCBH only; 1, 2) or
subjectively-assigned FSG (3, 4) models.

#### Upper canopy crowning


## Discussion

-We used an ensemble of 6 different sROS models for hemi-boreal stands,
using the *ISI*, *ISI~sa~*, or individual moisture and wind spe1ed
variables [@perrakis2026]: M12 (*ISI*), M13 (*ISI~sa~*), M16 (ws, FFMC),
M17 (ws, *mc~sa~*) , and M20% (ws), the latter being the 'mental
arithmetic' model that estimates sROS in conifer stands as 1.2% of the
open wind speed (or 20% of the wind speed in km h^-1^, expressed in m
min^-1^). While these sROS models suffer somewhat from sparse
observations for ISI \> \~12, typical crown fire conditions, they are
quite credible under conditions approximating our crowning thresholds of
*ISI*/ *ISI~sa~* of \~5-10. Approximate surface fire spread rate
predictions of 0.7 – 2.5 m min^-1^ are expected within this range of
conditions.

Aside from Van Wagner's equation, this is simply a slightly different
representation of Thomas' [-@thomas1963a] equation for flame size under
calm conditions.

\- Figure showing more complex architecture; 2-story stands, using Eq 2
to estimate contribution of surface fuels to upper stratum crowning -
Validation 4. Upper canopy crowning -Scale issues are obvious here.

-Calibration and solving for M relies on some assumptions from the
Sharpsand Creek site and previous studies by Stocks [@stocks1987] and
McRae et al. [@mcrae2017]. One of these is that the LCBH is essentially
identical in both IM and TH stands, approximately 4 m. More precise
analyses of raw survey data suggested a narrow range of values between
4.13 m and 4.94m for the IM stands at the time the fires were conducted,
producing the overall mean of 4.36 m. The thinning treatment in 5 of the
plots resulted in slightly higher DBH values, but was not believed to
have altered tree or overall stand height or LCBH; however, these values
were not measured precisely. The sensitivity of the equations to small
differences in these measures results in a certain amount of inherent
uncertainty with this post-hoc study design.

-A bit more sensitivity analyis on M is likely required. Probably need
to rerun M estimates using LCBH=4 for control plots and LCBH=4.5 for
thinned plots, as per DeGroot et al. (2022) (even though it's BS).

-Following the logic and intent of Van Wagner's (1977) model, the
scaling equation represents relationships between canopy strata
logically in 1-dimensional space, assuming ladder fuels are positioned
beneath overstory canopy fuels. They also may hold at the single tree
level, where individual ladder fuel elements (saplings, bark flakes,
arboreal lichen) are horizontally juxtaposed with overstory fuels. More
detailed survey methods [@alexander2004; @reinhardt2006a; @arkin2021]
can describe the frequency distributions associated with vertical strata
in a stand, while ecologists have described the spatial patterns of
overstory trees in conifer stands across various stand types
[@kenkel1997; @larson2012]. Future investigations will be needed on how
these spatial distribution patterns affect ladder fuel influences near
crown fire initiation thresholds.

-For the theoretical relationship to hold for actual ladder fuel
elements (flammable shrubs, saplings, bark flakes, hanging lichens,
etc.), it is imperative that they be connected to surface fuels, and in
actual forest settings this is uncertain. Factors such as flame
residence time (refs#) are probably important for determining the degree
of consumption of standing ladder fuels such as dead saplings.

-The concept of a multiplier for comparing elevated fuels to surface
fuels is a similar topic to Van Wagner's \[-vanwagner1977\] 'c'
parameter of 0.01, deduced from a comparison of only two experimental
fires, as discussed by Alexander [@alexander1998]. Densely-packed litter
fuelbeds have lower spread rate than lower density fuelbeds with the
same fuel load [@campbell-lochrie2021], although the relationship is
likely more complex in canopy fuels [@schwilk2015].

-As Andrews [-@andrews2018] noted, Rothermel surface model only
applicable to surface fuels, within \~6ft of the ground

-Thinning increases sub-canopy turbulence [@russell2018] and modelled
in-stand wind [@banerjee2020]

Method could also be used to estimate influence of dead branch fuel
below LCBH, bark flakes, arboreal lichens, or similar material.

Surface fire ROS model is an important component of all calculations.
Although the SROS models we present are imprecise and gloss over
potentially important differences such as litter type, canopy closure,
overstory species and porosity (as per Rothermel 1972; Campbell-Lochrie
et al. 2021), they are important to show real-world surface fire
conditions in Canadian conifer stands. These models can be used along
with crown fire modelling systems. In addition to the empirical models
shown here, SROS models can be used along with VW77, CanFire, CFIM, or
other tools appropriate to the context and questions of interest.

-What's actually going on in VW77 model: physics probably work (size of
flame under calm conditions, etc.), but SFC isn't instantaneous (only
part of it burns during flaming), and sROS needs to be realistic.

For example, Sharpsand thinned site stands (LCBH=4.4 m) had an ISI
threshold for crowning of 10.3. That ISI value is roughly associated
with ROS (using the M12 sROS model) of 2.86 m min^-1^. At a mean SFC of
1.377 kg m^-2^, Byram's (1959) model estimates that the fireline
intensity at 1181 kW/m intensity, well below the 1716 kW/m critical
intensity needed for crowning (at mean FMC of 108 %). While the physics
behind Van Wagner's model and 1993 analysis may be slightly overly
simplistic, the vertical relationship described here appears to work
well, when calibrated, as a method of objectively improving the accuracy
of crown fire occurrence models based on conifer stand structure and
fire weather conditions.

Only problem with the present effort that, as a calibration study, it
uses linkages between several empirical models, all of which appear
quite sensitive to inputs. Thus, sROS models are highly sensitive to
small differences in wind speed and fuel moisture, and the differences
in ISI thresholds between IM and TH stands can result in quite different
critical sROS values depending which model is chosen. The SFC and FC.se
are also sensitive and quite variable, with significant differences in
measured values between plots.

Supplemental Material

Sharpsand Creek: type of fire

There is a question of normalizing labels to identify which plots
experienced crown fire vs surface fire or transitional torching
behaviour. In the original Sharpsand experiments (1974-1981; IM and TH
stands: Stocks 1987; Cruz 1999), fire type was identified as 'surface'
or 'crown'. In the SM experiments, however, fire type was identified as
'surface', 'some torching', 'torching', and 'crown' [@mcrae2017].
Descriptions in the latter text make it clear that 'torching' fires
experienced behaviour akin to passive crowning, while those described as
'some torching' appeared to be near the crowning threshold (i.e.,
primarily surface fires but with \~5-15% crown fraction burned).
Following discussions with experimental leaders (BJ Stocks, pers. comm.
2020), the two fires described as 'some torching' were assumed to
bracket the crowning threshold: fire #16 (ISI=8.1, ROS=3.5 m/min) was
therefore considered to be best characterized as a surface fire
observation, while fire #18 (ISI=9.4, ROS=5.1 m/min) was characterized
as a marginal passive crown fire.
